newsitem.title: UK: Clarke speech points to modest tax cuts - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Clarke speech points to modest tax cuts - analysts.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's speech to the Conservative party conference suggests he will make modest tax cuts in his November 26 budget, economists said.
They said Clarke's insistence on the need for any tax cuts to be sustainable were a traditional pre-budget attempt to lower expectations and increase the impact of moderate reductions.

"What he is going to argue on budget day is that some tax reductions now are sustainable because he is able to cut public spending and keep public spending down over the medium term," said Gavyn Davies, chief economist at Goldman Sachs.
"Probably a one penny cut in the basic rate and a widening in the 20 pence band -- pretty much the same as he did last year -- is what we can expect again," he told Reuters Financial Television.

Davies, a member of Clarke's panel of independent economic advisers, said the chancellor had been very successful in controlling public spending, with almost no growth in real terms in the last three years.
"I think he can carry this on for at least another 12 months. I don't see any real emergency pressures that are developing in the short term to push public spending up."
"But I think over the medium term it is a lot more difficult because he is promising to keep real control-total spending growth on education and on health."
Glenn Davies, chief UK economist at Credit Lyonnais, said Clarke was keeping his cards close to his chest.

"The suspicion is that he will do something flashy on budget day, although it can't be a big give-away -- two to three billion stg in tax cuts is probably a reasonable guess," he said. "If he doesn't, his party won't like him for it." Davies said the economy did not need tax cuts but Clarke wanted to put "clear blue water" between himself and Labour.
"They will go for inheritance tax because Labour have said it is something they would reverse," Glenn Davies added.
In his speech, Clarke promised to reduce and eventually abolish both inheritance and capital gains tax.
Chris Tinker of Standard Chartered said there was no indication that Clarke would go soft on public expenditure.

"The fact that both fiscal and monetary policy are still essentially in the hands of one man -- the chancellor -- means that the markets will look extremely critically at how loose he wants to be with fiscal policy and will expect some monetary policy offset," he said.
"So if we do get tax cuts there will certainly be significant pressure for any rise in inflation to be met by tighter monetary policy," Tinker added.
"I think that's one of the reasons he's actually talking down expectations on fiscal policy at this stage."
